THE PERCEPTION OF VISUAL SURFACES
By JAMES J. GIBSON, Cornell University
The writer has recently proposed the theory that visual space-perception
is reducible to the perception of visual surfaces, and that distance, depth,
and orientation, together with the constancy of objects, may all be derived
from the properties of an array of surfaces.' The notion of completely
empty space is asserted to be irrelevant for the theory of space-perception.
The perception of space between objects, in this theory, depends on the
experience of contours against a general background, and on the impression
of one surface behind another. The fundamental 'sensations' of space are
assumed to be the impressions of surface and edge.
If the theory is valid, there should be discoverable variables in stimula-
tion for the essential properties or qualities of a surface, and these should
prove to be the effective stimuli for space-perception. What is called for is
a listing of the properties or qualities-a phenomenological study-and a
search for the corresponding stimulus variables-a program of psychophys-
ical experiments.
THE ESSENTIAL PROPERTIES OF A DETERMINATE VISUAL SURFACE
What, exactly, is a visual surface? The question is one for introspective
analysis. Perhaps the properties, qualities, or impressions which constitute
the experience of a surface can be specified. The properties sought for must
obviously be phenomenal properties which actually describe the perception,
not hypothetical elements such as points of color in a visual field. Con-
sidered in this way, a good deal of evidence has accumulated in the last
30 years which might provide an answer to the question. The contributions
to be considered are those of Katz,2 Rubin,3 Metzger,4 and Koffka.5

368 GIBSON
By a 'determinate visual surface' one should mean a section of the panorama of
surfaces which constitutes the ordinary visual scene. The face of an object is one
example. An airplane landing-strip is another. A table-top, or a lawn, or a roadway,
or a section of wall, or a floor are still others. The most fundamental surface, consti-
tuting the general background of all others, is the terrain extending to the horizon,
and this is a special case to which we shall recur. Surfaces are said to be 'determinate'
when they possess definite spatial qualities unlike the indeterminate extensity which
Katz named film-color. The cloudless sky is an example of the latter.
A tentative list of phenomenal properties. Subject to criticism and revi-
sion, the following list is suggested as composing the essential properties of
the experience of a determinate surface:
(1) The quality of being visually resistant, or 'hard.' Perhaps the most funda-
mental property of a surface is that it is solid to vision as well as to touch. This
discovery must be credited to Katz. In viewing a film color, he said, one feels as if
one could penetrate it whereas a surface has 'visual resistance.' Probably this is the
same thing as having texture, that is to say 'grain' or 'microstructure.' The evidence
points to that conclusion, but it is not yet certain. Subject to verification, the term
texture will be used as if these properties were identical. Texture is a variable. Its
primary variation is between coarse and dense. It has other qualitative dimensions ,of
course, but these are as yet unspecified. Texture needs to be redescribed and the
stimulus-conditions for it need to be discovered. It is certainly based on inhomo-
geneous retinal stimulation, as Koffka suggested,6 but a more exact statement than
this should be formulable. Research on visual acuity should be valuable in this
connection.
(2) The qualities of extended color. These would include brightness (more
accurately, whiteness-blackness) and hue and saturation. Surface-colors are insepara-
ble from texture and are localized in space, the color adhering to the slopes and
curves of the surface in question. Color of this sort manifests 'constancy.'
(3) The property of being illuminated or darkened, i.e. lighted or shadowed. It
might be more accurate to combine this quality with the previous one and to speak
of a surface as having a color-in-a-given-illumination.7
(4) The quality of slant. Any surface or segment of a surface has a visible slope
or, to define it differently, faces in a certain direction. A surface having the same
slant in all parts is flat; one having differing slants in different parts is curved or
bent. Slant is a simple impression. This impression can be defined most simply as
angular inclination to the line of regard. It varies in opposite directions from the
neutral quality of 'straight in front' (the so-called 'frontal plane') toward the two
extreme qualities represented by a floor and a ceiling, and the two other extreme
qualities represented by a right-hand wall and a left-hand wall. Slant may be said
to vary in amount and in direction. Adjacent variations of slant yield higher-order
6Koffka, op. cit., 110 ff.
7 Katz, in the reference cited, has distinguished still other variable properties of a
surface besides color and illumination, notably 'pronouncedness' and 'impressive-
ness.' Since these phenomenal qualities may be predicted, however, from the proper-
ties now being listed, they need not be given the status of essential properties.

PERCEPTION OF VISUAL SURFACES 369
qualities such as concavity or convexity, protuberance or indentation, sharpness or
roundness, and many others.
The fact is, of course, that we perceive not only the slant of a surface to the line
of sight but the slant of a surface to the plane of the ground-its inclination to the
horizontal and vertical axes determined by gravity. A surface is normally oriented
in objective space. This latter impression, however, seems to depend on the main-
taining of equilibrium by the observer as well as on purely visual stimulation.' The
simpler type of impression should probably be investigated first. It will here be
called 'optical slant' as distinguished from 'gravitational slant.'
(5) The property of nearness or farness, or distance. Any segment of the world
has a visible distance, which varies from zero to a maximum. According to the
writer's theory, the impression of distance depends on a continuous background
surface on which the segment in question appears. Usually this is the ground; al-
though floor, walls and ceiling are also background surfaces in artificial environ-
ments. The ground fills the ordinary visual field continuously downward until it
adjoins the projection of the observer's nose and body. If such a ground-surface is
lacking, as when one looks upward into a clear sky, the impression of determinate
distance is also lacking.
(6) The impression of a closed contour. Most of the surfaces of the phenomenal
world are delimited, and the experience of objects is made possible by this fact.
Object-surfaces are separated from their background by a closed contour. The special
case of the ground itself (or of any surface filling the entire visual field) which does
not have a closed contour, will be considered later. The bounding contour of a
surface does not seem to be a variable property as are the others being described, and it
is not measurable as the others are. It tends to produce an entity or things in experience
rather than a quality.
(7) The quality of shape-at-a-given-slant. A closed contour always has a shape.
Although a contour is a fact, the shape of a contour is a variable. Shape varies along
a vast number of dimensions for most of which there are no terms. We apply words
only to certain common or standard shapes, but the fact is that there are transitional
shapes between any one and any other.' Although the variables of shape are not
measurable in any known uits, it is not inconceivable that they might become so by
the application of methods derived from projective geometry.
It should be noted that the quality of shape is inseparably linked with the quality
of slant already described. Shape is not possible without a contour and a contour is
inseparable from a surface. Disembodied geometrical forms are abstractions which
do not concern the present inquiry. Outlines drawn on paper, being atypical and
artificial, are likewise irrelevant. The kind of shape which is attached to a surface
manifests so-called 'constancy.'
(8) The quality of size-at-a-given-distance. Any contoured surface is characterized
by size. Size may vary from zero to a maximum. It is measurable on either of two
dimensions, width or height, and when both dimensions are perceived jointly a new
property emerges: namely, area.
It is impossible for an impression of size to occur without an impression of

Psychol. Rev., 45, 1938, 300-323.
Gibson, The Perception of the Visual World, Chap. 10.

370 GIBSON
distance. Size is inseparable from distance, just as shape is linked with slant. Im-
pressions of size, like impressions of shape, tend to be objectively correct over the
whole visual environment.
These eight properties of a visual surface, or some revised set, may be
thought of as essential. Any surface should possess all of them, texture, color
and illumination, slant, distance, contour, shape-at-a-slant, and size-at-a-
distance, and together they should be sufficient to constitute a surface. It
remains to be considered how these impressions can arise in perception. The
striking fact about these phenomenal properties is that, although they are
mediated entirely by retinal images, they are generally in good correspond-
ence with the 'exact' properties of the physical surface in question when the
latter are measured by instruments. This fact expresses in a somewhat novel
form the problem of visual space-perception.
The case of a surface without visible contour. In certain circumstances
one may perceive a surface lacking a determinate contour.
If an O stands close enough to a large wall without moving his head the surface
will fill nearly the entire visual field and its edges will become invisible.'0 A curved
screen (cyclorama) can be arranged to extend over the whole visual field. Since the
surface has no visible contour it also has no shape and no size. It has texture, and
may have the remaining qualities in the list; but the latter supposition has never been
investigated.
A uniform surface may also be viewed through a hole or tube which restricts the
visual field and makes the margins of the surface invisible. Either a surface or a
film may be seen, depending on the size of the hole, the nature and illumination of
the surface structure, and the distances of the hole and the surface from O. Assuming
the angle of view to be large and the window to be near the eye, O perceives the
closed contour of the window as separated from and in front of the surface. The
surface extends behind the window and has no determinate contour, shape or size. It
has texture, surface-color, slant and distance. This report has been verified by several
Os in the course of exploratory experiments connected with the present project.
One may also view a surface through a small window at some distance from the
eye. This is the 'aperture-screen' experiment. If the surface is a substantial distance
behind the aperture, it loses nearly all of its properties and is usually no longer a
surface but a film-color. The area within the hole has hue, brightness, and saturation,
but no texture and no protuberances or indentations. It has no contour, shape, size
or slant except those of the surface in which the hole is cut. Its apparent distance is
simply the distance of that surface.
The first and last of these experiments (the wall and the aperture-screen) are
those of Metzger and of Katz, already referred to. The second has apparently not
been studied. The transition between the determinate surface and the indeterminate
film needs to be investigated. Metzger produced this transition by reducing the illum-
ination on a wall filling the visual field, the Ganzfeld, but it might also be obtaina-
ble by other means, such as gradually reducing the angular size of an aperture.
0 Metzger, op. cit., 10 ff.

PERCEPTION OF VISUAL SURFACES 371
THE VERIFICATION OF HYPOTHETICAL STIMULUS-CORRELATES FOR
TEXTURE, SLANT, AND DISTANCE
One may adopt the working hypothesis that the spatial properties of
phenomenal surfaces are in correspondence with variables of retinal stimu-
lation. This would mean, for instance, that the 'cues' for distance-percep-
tion have been misconceived and should be reformulated as quantities.
Moreover the quantities should all have reference to a surface or to some
relation between surfaces. If we could account for the solidity of a surface,
the slant of a surface, the continuously increasing distance of the ground-
surface, and the distance at which one surface lies in front of another, we
should have gone a long way toward explaining the visual world in terms
of stimulation.
It is a reasonable hypothesis that only if a visual impression hasr the
peculiar hardness of a surface can it have the other properties of slant and
relative distance. Conceivably this hardness depends on the fundamental
property of texture. Distance may be given by the relative density of tex-
ture, the finer the density the greater being the distance. Slant at any point
may be given by the rate of increase of density of the texture at that point.
Perspective, in this theory, reduces to the increasing condensation of the
projected elements of the physical environment-a gradient of density along
a meridian of the retina.
The remaining cues for depth likewise all presuppose a 'textured' retinal
image. The important ones can be reduced to variable quantities or gradi-
ents based on texture-elements. Motion parallax considered as a correlate
of continuous distance, or the recession of a surface, is the gradient of
deformation of the elements of the image when the head moves. The
stereoscopic cue, considered in this way, is the gradient of relative disparity
of the elements in the binocular images.1l
The stimulus for texture. The retinal correlate of texture might be adja-
cent cycles of intensity in the image. A surface, as contrasted with a film-
color, might correspond to an image composed of speckled instead of
homogeneous light, i.e. spots of alternating light and dark, which are
reportable as 'grain' or microstructure. In order to verify this hypothesis,
experiments would have to show, first, that the peculiar hardness or solidity
of a surface is always accompanied by texture and, secondly, that whenever
an O's retina was stimulated by the appropriate kind of speckled light he
would report the hardness of a surface.
1 Gibson, The Perception of the Visual World, Chap. 6, 7, has an account of these
cues reformulated as gradients of stimulation.

372 GIBSON
The experiments of Metzger on stimulation over the entire visual field
need to be repeated in order to study specifically what kind of stimulation
yields a film and what kind yields a surface. If the transition between a
surface and a film can be produced by one or more techniques of reducing
the angular size of a window, this method should be also employed. Since
a textured image is probably an image with 'definition' or 'resolution,'
optical methods of artificially focussing and unfocussing the retinal image
may also be revealing.
The stimuli for distance. The hypothesis is that the impression of dis-
tance at any point on a receding surface is a function of the density of the
texture-elements in that region, relative to the maximal and minimal densi-
ties over the entire image. This variable may be supplemented by two
others, contingent on head-movement and binocular vision respectively.
(The impression of depth, unlike most other phenomenal qualities, ordi-
narily has multiple stimuli.) The two supplementary variables are relative
deformation of texture-elements and relative disparity of the congruent
elements in the two images. They can be eliminated, however, by requiring
monocular observation with a motionless head, or by the expedient of
stimulating the eye with a picture, that is, with elements artificially pro-
duced on a frontal surface.
To verify this hypothesis a number of experiments are needed. It would
have to be shown that a retinal gradient of texture-density, in isolation
from the two other gradients, yields the impression of a receding surface.
A simple psychophysical experiment could be set up to determine whether,
of two adjacent segments of surface in the visual field, that with the denser
texture is seen the more distant. It could also be determined whether the
greater the difference in this density the farther will one segment appear
behind the other at their mutual contour.
The demonstration that the variable of relative motion and that of
binocular disparity are, in isolation, effective stimuli for distance ought to
be made but the experiment is not so straightforward. They can be iso-
lated from one another but neither can be isolated from texture in the
most general sense of the term. Nevertheless there is evidence that the
'cues' of disparity and motion parallax are effective. A kind of disembodied
distance is obtained in stereoscopic experiments with lines and points when
the perspective of the lines and points would locate them in a frontal
plane. A gradient of disparity can be made to conflict with a zero gradient
of texture by the use of 'meridianal size-lenses,' described by Ogle12 and
12K. N. Ogle, The induced size effect, J. Opt. Soc., 30, 1940, 145-151.

PERCEPTION OF VISUAL SURFACES 373-
Ames,13 and the result is an 'illusory' slant on a frontal surface. This ex-
periment should be carried out systematically. The attempt should also be
made to study motion parallax using lines and points in the same way
that binocular parallax has been studied with the stereoscope. This experi-
ment has apparently not been performed.
The stimuli for slant. The apparent slant of a surface to the line of re-
gard at any point might be given by the rate of increase of the density of
elements at the corresponding point in the image. The direction of the
slant would correspond to the direction of the gradient. This variable,
like the variable of density proper, may be supplemented by the gradient
of deformation-motion and the gradient of binocular disparity, but these
can be experimentally eliminated. The variable of the contour of the sur-
face and its shape can also be eliminated by the use of a hole-screen.
In order to verify this hypothesis it would be necessary to project on the
retina of an O a small textured image such as would be projected by a
segment of a physical surface having a certain angle to the line of sight.
The texture of the image should be varied on different occasions with re-
spect to the gradient of its texture, increasing in density from left to right,
top to bottom, etc., and sometimes not changing in density at all. It is
predicted that O will perceive a slanted surface in these circumstances. He
can be required to reproduce the direction and the amount of the apparent
slant with some convenient device. If the direction and amount of the
gradient of density prove to be in correspondence with the direction and
amount of the slant as reproduced, it could be asserted that the gradient
was a stimulus for the quality experienced.
The factor of texture-density could be isolated from the factors of dis-
parity and motion by stimulating the eye with a picture of a segment of a
physical surface-either drawn or photographed. The margins of the
picture could be eliminated by viewing it through a hole.
We have here suggested a program of experiments to test the general
hypothesis that solidity, slant, and distance, three of the suggested proper-
ties of a visual surface, are in psychophysical correspondence with variables
of retinal stimulation. The stimuli proposed are derivatives of adjacent
cycles of intensity over the retinal image, or what may loosely be called
'speckled light.' A number of the experiments designed to verify such
stimuli will be reported subsequently as part of a general project. Here
we consider slant.

374 GIBSON
THE PROPERTY OF SLANT
On the assumption that the impression of a visual surface depends upon
a textured retinal image or in other words a 'speckled' distribution of light,
it is a reasonable hypothesis that the impression of the slant of a surface
at the point fixated depends on the rate of change of the density of this
texture at the fovea.14 This hypothesis is reasonable because, according
to the geometry of perspective, a physical surface not perpendicular to the
line of sight does of necessity project a distribution of texture-elements
which gets denser as the surface recedes, and whose gradient of density
is proportional to the angle of slant.l5 The rule is nothing more than an
application of geometry to the texture of a surface instead of to the outline
of a surface. Conventional perspective has always been confined to the
latter but there is no good reason for this limitation. Given this physical
fact it seems possible that animals may respond to such a gradient of den-
sity over the retina by seeing a surface in depth. The hypothesis could be
verified for man by projecting a textured image into one eye and demon-
strating that, as the gradient of density was increased by E, the slant of the
perceived surface was reported to increase correspondingly. The effect of
a textured image having the same density at all points should be an im-
pression of no slant, i.e. a surface in the frontal plane. The purpose of the
experiment to be reported was to test this hypothesis.
Phenomenal variable of slant. A visual surface has two kinds of per-
ceptible slant. One kind has reference to the line of sight from the eye
to the surface. It is definable as inclination to this line, or rotation of the
surface around either of two axes perpendicular to this line-the right-
left axis and the top-bottom axis. These axes refer to O's head and eyes
whatever his posture may be. The other kind of perceptible slant has
reference to the line of gravity and to the absolute axes of the physical
environment (for example, north-south and east-west). The first will be
called 'optical slant' and the second 'gravitational slant.'
The page of a book as one ordinarily holds it in reading has a zero optical slant
but a 45? gravitational slant. Both kinds are perceived and both need to be accounted
for, but the slant with which this experiment is concerned is optical only. In the
optical sense of the term, a surface, or any fixated segment of a surface, may slant
forward or backward and to the right or to the left. Since the variables are contin-
uous it is preferable to say that optical slant may vary along two independent dimen-
sions each having opposite directions, ceilingwise or floorwise, and right wallward,
or left wallward. A ceilingwise slant recedes downwards, a floorwise slant upwards;
14 Gibson, The Perception of Visual Surfaces, see the Introduction.
15 Gibson, idem, Chap. 5 and 6.

PERCEPTION OF VISUAL SURFACES 375
a right wall recedes to the left, and a left wall recedes to the right. There may
of course exist combinations or mixtures of these qualities. The variables of slant are
comparable to the variables of hue, which have pairs of complementary colors with
a neutral quality in the middle.
The hypothesis predicts that an increase in the density of texture up-
ward in the visual field yields a floorwise slant (a slant backward) and an
increase downward, a ceilingwise slant (a slant forward); that an increase
in density to the right yields a left wallward slant, and an increase to the
left a right wallward slant.16
Isolation of the texture-gradient. The slant of a visual surface in the
region fixated may also depend on gradients of stimulation which are
supplementary to the gradient of texture-density. The gradient of binocular
disparity and the gradient of relative motion when O's head moves are,
equally with density of texture, in an exact geometrical correspondence to
the slant of a physical surface to the line of sight.l7 In order to show that
the texture-gradient can be an effective determiner of phenomenal slant in
isolation, these supplementary gradients must be eliminated from the ex-
periment. 0, in other words, must be stimulated only by an undeforming
retinal image confined to a single eye.
In ordinary perception, the surfaces we see possess contours. The face
of an object, for instance, has a closed shape. Since many of the surfaces
of civilized environments have rectangular contours, or at least familiar
shapes, the perspective of the outline of a surface is frequently a genuine
cue to its optical slant. In order to eliminate this cue in the present ex-
periment, the contour of the surface must be rendered invisible. If we are
to avoid the complexities of the problem of shape-constancy, the surface

Apparatus. The apparatus is represented in Fig. 1. Differential blur and accommo-
dation are eliminated by projecting a sharp image on a translucent screen and allow-
ing this image to be projected on the retina of a single eye. This arrangement at
the same time eliminates differential motions in the image (the gradient of relative
motion) and differences in disparity between binocular images. The impression of a
contour attached to the surface is eliminated by using a pair of hole-screens near
the eye, the margin of the circular hole (24? in diam.) being out of focus.
With head fixed, O looks monocularly through two hole-screens at a translucent
projection-screen on which a photographic image is projected. The angle subtended
by this image at the eye is equal to the angle of the scene subtended at the lens
of the camera which made the photograph. In other words, O views the projected
image at such a distance as to make his retinal image the same size as the hypothetical
image he would have got by placing his eye in the position of the camera lens.
The dimensions are given with Fig. 1.

The apparatus arrangement was such that the physical slant equivalent to the

The screen was a thin sheet of fine-grained translucent plexiglass. Its own texture
(which had of course a contradictory gradient to that of the projected image) was
barely visible under high illumination. Nevertheless it is possible that this fact had
an effect on the results. The absence of differential blur in the image itself (since all
parts of the projected image were equally in focus on the frontal projection-screen)
also operated in contradiction to the gradient of texture-density in that it favored
the perception of the zero slant of the screen itself. The cues of motion parallax and
binocular disparity, had they been present, would also have been determinants
favoring perception of a frontal surface. But since a headrest was used to keep the
eye motionless during observations and since viewing was monocular, we assume
that these cues did not play a contradictory r6le. The scene yielded a rather com-
pelling impression of a slanted surface.19
Procedure. The apparent slant of the surface perceived on each trial was recorded
by the method of reproduction. The device used was a 6-in. square of composition-
board fixed at eye-level in a convenient position for adjustment by O's right hand.
It could be rotated 90? backward or forward from a vertical plane. O adjusted the
movable surface with his palm until the tactual-kinesthetic impression was the same
as the visual impression. Slants were recorded to the nearest degree.
Prior to the presentation of each stimulus the board was moved to one of four pre-
settings, 25? or 55? backward and 25? or 55? forward. These were distributed
equally for the 16 standard stimuli, each pre-setting being used four times for each.20
After a practice series of one judgment for each standard stimulus, 16 judgments
for each of the 16 stimuli were obtained. Rest-periods were provided after every 48
judgments. Four orders of the standard stimuli were used four times each in a varied
sequence. In each order there was an alternation between regular and irregular tex-
ture and between backward and forward slant.
Ten paid Os participated in the experiment, the entire procedure taking about
3 hr. for each. Nine of these were women (3 students, 3 clerical workers, 3 psy-
chology teachers): the man was an engineer.

To assert that the gradient of texture-density is a stimulus-correlate of
perceived optical slant might involve the assumption that this response to
a gradient is a response to a mathematical property of the texture inde-
pendent of the particular texture itself, just as a melody is independent
of specific notes. There is evidence, however, that the kind of texture does
affect this response. It has been shown to influence the degree of differential
sensitivity: the degree to which the gradient can function as a slant deter-
minant. A regular texture gives a clearer impression of slant than does a
less regular. Possibly a regular texture affords a more definite gradient of
density than does an irregular texture.
The discrepancy between the judged slant and the 'physical slant equiv-
alent to the gradient' is consistently in the direction of a frontal surface.
The judged slants were compromises. As has already been pointed out, the
visibility of the texture of the projection-screen, together with the absence
of differential blur and the resulting absence of the cue of accommodation,
would favor such a compromise between a slanted and a frontal impres-
sion. Other factors which may also have contributed to this 'frontal
tendency' are the tendency of the perception to conform to the slant of the
hole-screen and any residual head-motion not eliminated by the headrest.
An artifact of the method by which the data have been treated should be pointed
out. In Fig. 3 there is a greater discrepancy between the judged slant and the 'physical
slant equivalent to the gradient' in A than B. In A one of the means is even slightly
below the abscissa, which would seem to indicate a slight slant forward for an up-
ward texture-density increase. This is a consequence of using the objective vertical of
the adjustable board as the baseline. A better baseline would be the position of the
board as judged vertical by 0, or what could be called the tactual-kinesthetic vertical
for the set-up used. This was empirically determined by having each O make 4 such
adjustments at the end of his observing period. The mean of these judgments is
4.1? forward (ceilingwise) relative to the objective vertical, with a standard devia-
tion of 5.4?. The curves in Fig. 3 can be corrected for this discrepancy between the
gravitational and the tactual-kinesthetic vertical by raising each mean in A by 4.1?
and lowering each mean in B by the same amount. When this is done the discrep-
ancy between the two curves disappears.

phenomenal environment can be similarly accounted for when an appro-
